/-!
# Steiner Systems

A Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$ is a collection of $k$-element subsets (called blocks) of
an $n$-element set such that every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steiner_system)
- [Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems)
  by Kunal Marwaha
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace SteinerSystems

/--
An $S(t, k, n)$-Steiner system is a collection of $k$-element subsets (called blocks) of
$\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ such that every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.

This is the standard notation from combinatorics, where:
- $n$ is the number of points
- $k$ is the block size
- $t$ is the covering parameter (every $t$-subset is in exactly one block)
-/
structure SteinerSystem (t k n : ℕ) where
  /-- The blocks of the Steiner system. -/
  blocks : Finset (Finset (Fin n))
  /-- Every block has exactly $k$ elements. -/
  block_card : ∀ B ∈ blocks, B.card = k
  /-- Every $t$-element subset is contained in exactly one block.
  Note: We use `.filter.card = 1` instead of `∃!` because `∃! B ∈ blocks, R ⊆ B` desugars to
  a quantifier over all `Finset (Fin n)`, which loses `Decidable` and breaks `native_decide`. -/
  cover_unique : ∀ R : Finset (Fin n), R.card = t → (blocks.filter (R ⊆ ·)).card = 1

/-- Notation for Steiner systems: `S(t, k, n)` denotes a Steiner system with
covering parameter `t`, block size `k`, and `n` points. -/
scoped notation "S(" t ", " k ", " n ")" => SteinerSystem t k n

/--
A constructive witness for a large Steiner system: concrete values of $n$, $k$, $t$
satisfying $n > k > t > 5$, $t < 10$, $n < 200$, together with an explicit Steiner system.
-/
structure LargeSteinerSystemWitness where
  /-- The size of the ground set. -/
  n : ℕ
  /-- The block size. -/
  k : ℕ
  /-- The covering parameter. -/
  t : ℕ
  h_nk : n > k
  h_kt : k > t
  h_t_lower : t > 5
  h_t_upper : t < 10
  h_n_upper : n < 200
  /-- The explicit Steiner system. -/
  system : S(t, k, n)

/--
Construct an $S(t, k, n)$-Steiner system with $n > k > t > 5$, $t < 10$, and $n < 200$.

No example of a Steiner system with $t > 5$ is known, despite a 2014 existence theorem
by Keevash showing that such systems must exist for sufficiently large $n$.

*Reference:* [Large Steiner Systems](https://epoch.ai/frontiermath/open-problems/large-steiner-systems)
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem large_steiner_systems : Nonempty LargeSteinerSystemWitness := by
  sorry

/--
Sanity check: the Fano plane is an $S(2, 3, 7)$-Steiner system.

The Fano plane consists of $7$ blocks of size $3$ over $7$ points,
where every pair of points is contained in exactly one block.
-/
@[category test, AMS 5]
def fano_plane : S(2, 3, 7) :=
  ⟨{{(0 : Fin 7), 1, 3}, {1, 2, 4}, {2, 3, 5},
    {3, 4, 6}, {0, 4, 5}, {1, 5, 6}, {0, 2, 6}},
   by native_decide, by native_decide⟩

/--
**Existence of $S(5, 8, 24)$**: The large Witt design.

There exists a unique Steiner system $S(5, 8, 24)$, known as the large Witt design.
It was constructed by Witt (1938) and is closely related to the Mathieu group $M_{24}$.
This is one of only two known Steiner systems with $t = 5$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem steiner_system_5_8_24 : Nonempty S(5, 8, 24) := by
  sorry

/--
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 4$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
Since there are infinitely many such admissible $n$, this implies infinitely many
$S(4, k, n)$ systems exist (for any fixed $k > 4$). The proof is nonconstructive.

Explicit examples include $S(4, 5, 11)$ (the unique system, related to the Mathieu
group $M_{11}$) and $S(4, 7, 23)$ (related to the Mathieu group $M_{23}$).

Only nontrivial systems with $4 < k < n$ are counted: for every $n$ the single block
$\{1, \dots, n\}$ is an $S(4, n, n)$, and all $4$-subsets of an $n$-set form an $S(4, 4, n)$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem infinitely_many_steiner_t4 :
    {s : Σ k n : ℕ, S(4, k, n) | 4 < s.1 ∧ s.1 < s.2.1}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
**There are infinitely many Steiner systems with $t = 5$.**

Keevash (2014) proved that for any fixed $t$ and $k$, a Steiner system $S(t, k, n)$
exists for all sufficiently large $n$ satisfying the necessary divisibility conditions.
This settles the long-standing open problem of whether infinitely many $S(5, k, n)$
systems exist. The proof is nonconstructive.

Only two explicit examples are known: $S(5, 6, 12)$ and $S(5, 8, 24)$, both Witt
designs related to the Mathieu groups $M_{12}$ and $M_{24}$ respectively.

Only nontrivial systems with $5 < k < n$ are counted, for the same reason as in
`infinitely_many_steiner_t4`.
No Steiner system with $t \geq 6$ has been explicitly constructed, though Keevash's
result guarantees their existence nonconstructively as well.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5]
theorem infinitely_many_steiner_t5 :
    {s : Σ k n : ℕ, S(5, k, n) | 5 < s.1 ∧ s.1 < s.2.1}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end SteinerSystems

findings.description: The docstring says "This is one of only two known Steiner systems with $t = 5$" (meaning S(5,6,12) and S(5,8,24)). That is false. Several other explicit Steiner 5-designs have long been known, e.g. S(5,6,24), S(5,7,28), S(5,6,48), S(5,6,84) (Denniston 1976), S(5,6,72) and more. The Lean statement `Nonempty S(5, 6, 12)` and its proof are unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: Marwaha's Steiner Systems List (https://marwahaha.github.io/steinersystems/), reference [7] of the Epoch write-up. Its table marks S(5,6,24) as known ("There is a known Steiner system S(5, 6, 24) ... which induces S(4, 5, 23)") and says "KNOWN: We know of Steiner systems at S(5, 6, 36) and S(5, 6, 48)". It cites Denniston, "Some New 5-Designs", Bull. London Math. Soc. 8(3) (1976) 263 (title confirmed via Crossref). Wikipedia's Steiner system article lists known S(4,5,n) for n = 23, 35, 47, 71, …, 243. Keevash (arXiv:1401.3665, intro) says only that "there were only finitely many known Steiner systems with r ≥ 4", not two.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the sentence with e.g. "Only finitely many Steiner systems with $t = 5$ are known explicitly, among them $S(5,6,12)$, $S(5,8,24)$, $S(5,6,24)$, $S(5,7,28)$ and $S(5,6,48)$." Alternatively, delete it.

findings.description: The docstring says "Only two explicit examples are known: $S(5, 6, 12)$ and $S(5, 8, 24)$". This is false: more explicit Steiner systems with t = 5 are known, e.g. S(5,6,24), S(5,7,28) and S(5,6,48). The Lean statement (the set of nontrivial S(5,k,n) is infinite) is unaffected and correct.

reformulations.difference: The Lean asserts that a set of Σ-type elements ⟨k, n, S⟩ is infinite: labelled systems S on Fin n with 4 < k < n. The source (Wikipedia) asks whether infinitely many nontrivial (t < k < n) Steiner systems have t = 4, i.e. for infinitely many orders / up to isomorphism.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A `SteinerSystem t k n` is determined by its `blocks : Finset (Finset (Fin n))`, so each type SteinerSystem t k n is finite. Since k < n, only finitely many (k, n) pairs arise below any bound on n. Hence the Σ-set is infinite iff {n | ∃ k, 4 < k ∧ k < n ∧ Nonempty S(4,k,n)} is infinite. That in turn holds iff there are infinitely many isomorphism classes of nontrivial S(4,k,n), since isomorphic systems share (k, n) and each (k, n) has finitely many systems. The condition 4 < k < n excludes exactly the trivial S(4,4,n) and S(4,n,n) families.

reformulations.difference: Same form as the t = 4 case: an infinite set of labelled Σ-elements ⟨k, n, S⟩ with 5 < k < n, versus the source's "infinitely many nontrivial Steiner systems have t = 5".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The same argument applies: each SteinerSystem 5 k n is finite (determined by its blocks) and k < n. The Σ-set is therefore infinite iff infinitely many n admit a nontrivial S(5,k,n), iff there are infinitely many isomorphism classes. Proved in Lean as `reform 5` (checked against `type_of% @infinitely_many_steiner_t5`).

reformulations.difference: Epoch asks to "find" (exhibit) an (n,q,r)-Steiner system with n > q > r > 5, r < 10, n < 200. The Lean asserts `Nonempty LargeSteinerSystemWitness`, the existence of such data.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: `Nonempty LargeSteinerSystemWitness` ↔ ∃ n k t, n > k ∧ k > t ∧ t > 5 ∧ t < 10 ∧ n < 200 ∧ Nonempty S(t,k,n); I proved this unpacking in Lean. The Epoch parameters map as q ↦ k and r ↦ t, with all bounds strict as in the prompt. The search space is finite (n < 200, blocks on Fin n), so existence is equivalent to an explicit example existing. The existence claim is the conjecture implicit in the construction task; it would be negated if disproved.

sources_consulted: https://arxiv.org/e-print/1401.3665 (Keevash, The existence of designs, LaTeX source)
review.notes:
No misformalization found. Details:

- The current `infinitely_many_steiner_t4` / `_t5` correctly exclude trivial systems. With the 4 < k < n (resp. 5 < k < n) condition, the statements are equivalent (proved in scratch Lean) to "infinitely many n admit a nontrivial S(t,k,n)". This is exactly the consequence of Keevash's theorem. None of it is trivially provable, since for t = 4, 5 no explicit infinite families are known.
- `large_steiner_systems` matches the Epoch prompt verbatim: n > q > r > 5, r < 10, n < 200. Epoch lists it as "Unsolved", so `research open` is current. Every other status in the file also matches its source: Keevash 2014 for t = 4, 5; the Witt designs are classical.
- `steiner_system_5_6_12` and `fano_plane` rely on `native_decide`. I re-checked both with an independent `#eval` on a copy of the block list. S(5,6,12): 132 blocks, all of size 6, and 0 of the 792 5-subsets fail to lie in exactly one block. Fano plane: 7 blocks, and every pair lies in exactly one block.
- Minor historical nuance, not filed: Wikipedia says S(5,8,24) "was first described by Carmichael (1931) and rediscovered by Witt (1938)". The docstring's "constructed by Witt (1938)" omits Carmichael but is not wrong as such.
- Omission, not a defect: Wikipedia's third item, the existence of nontrivial Steiner systems with t ≥ 6 (solved by Keevash), is not stated separately. Only the stronger, still-open Epoch variant with n < 200, t ≤ 9 appears.
